response: Multi-label text classification – the task of assigning multiple, potentially overlapping categories to a given text – is a fundamental problem in natural language processing with applications ranging from news categorization and topic detection to medical diagnosis and legal document analysis. While significant progress has been made in recent years leveraging deep learning models (Yang et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2016), a crucial challenge often overlooked in practice is the long-tailed distribution of labels within large-scale datasets. Real-world multi-label datasets typically exhibit a power-law distribution, characterized by a small number of frequent labels and a vast majority of infrequent or entirely unseen labels. This poses a significant problem for traditional supervised learning approaches, which struggle to generalize to less represented categories, leading to poor performance on a substantial portion of the label space. Specifically, a large multi-label dataset can be naturally partitioned into three groups: (1) *frequent labels* appearing thousands of times, where standard supervised methods perform reasonably well; (2) *few-shot labels* occurring only a handful of times, where generalization is severely limited due to data scarcity; and (3) *zero-shot labels* completely absent from the training data, presenting a challenge for any model trained solely on observed categories. The imbalanced nature of these label distributions introduces a substantial bias towards frequent labels, effectively marginalizing the prediction accuracy of infrequent and unseen categories. This is especially true in specialized domains like medical text classification, where the number of potential diagnoses or conditions can be very large, and the training data often lacks sufficient examples for rare diseases or procedures. Existing research addressing few-shot and zero-shot learning largely focuses on image classification (Fei-Fei et al., 2006; Russell et al., 2006) or single-label text classification (Yao et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2019). While techniques such as meta-learning and metric learning have shown promise, their application to the multi-label setting – especially when dealing with structured label spaces – remains largely unexplored. Furthermore, most previous work lacks a comprehensive, fine-grained evaluation of existing methods on infrequent labels, creating a gap in understanding their actual performance limitations. In this paper, we address the problem of few-shot and zero-shot multi-label learning for structured label spaces, focusing on text classification in the medical domain. We present a thorough evaluation of state-of-the-art methods on two publicly available datasets – MIMIC II and MIMIC III – demonstrating their shortcomings on infrequent labels. Building upon these insights, we develop novel approaches that leverage the inherent hierarchical structure often present in medical taxonomies (e.g., ICD codes) to improve prediction accuracy for both few-shot and zero-shot categories. Our results demonstrate significant performance gains compared to prior efforts, achieving improvements of up to 6.2% and 17.3% in Recall@10 for few-shot and zero-shot labels, respectively, establishing a new benchmark for this challenging task.

response: Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD), the task of identifying the correct meaning (sense) of a word in context, has remained a central challenge in Natural Language Processing for decades. Despite significant progress in machine learning and computational linguistics, achieving high accuracy on all words and all senses remains elusive. A primary obstacle is the inherent ambiguity of natural language and the uneven distribution of word senses – some senses are far more frequent than others. Traditional WSD systems, even those leveraging sophisticated machine learning techniques like supervised learning with rich features (e.g., Lesk algorithm variations, feature-based classifiers), consistently exhibit poor performance on low-frequency senses (Atkins & Zernack, 1991; Kilgarriff, 1997). This is largely attributable to a fundamental data imbalance: training corpora often lack sufficient examples of rarer senses, leading the models to favor more prevalent interpretations, even when those are contextually inappropriate. Early attempts to address this issue focused on enriching training data. This involved expanding existing resources like WordNet (Miller, 1995) with additional sense definitions, or creating larger annotated corpora through expensive and time-consuming manual annotation efforts (e.g., SemCor, Navigli & Ponzetto, 2009). Knowledge-based approaches, aiming to utilize lexical resources to infer sense relationships, also gained traction. While these methods contributed to incremental improvements, they often struggled with scalability and the inherent limitations of manually curated knowledge. More recently, approaches concentrating on sense induction – automatically discovering senses from large unlabeled corpora – have become increasingly popular (Lin, 1998; Jalili & Vanderwende, 2010). These methods seek to alleviate the data scarcity problem by leveraging the vast quantities of readily available text. However, the quality and representativeness of the induced senses, as well as the effectiveness of aligning them with established sense inventories like WordNet, can vary considerably. A growing trend has also centered around identifying and prioritizing a limited set of predominant senses for each word, effectively reducing the ambiguity space (Zheng & Manandhar, 2012). However, a critical, yet often overlooked, aspect lies in the *characteristics* of the training data itself. Beyond simply acquiring more data or inducing new senses, the volume of data, its origin (provenance), and crucially, how sense distributions within the training data align with those in the test data, are all potentially influential factors. This paper directly investigates the impact of these ‘meta-properties’ of training data on WSD performance. We hypothesize that an artificially unbalanced training corpus, even with a large number of examples, can lead to suboptimal results if it does not adequately capture the relative frequencies of different senses, as they appear in real-world text. We demonstrate, through experimentation on the SemEval-2013 English all-words task, that careful balancing of sense distributions in the training data can significantly boost performance, exceeding state-of-the-art results by a substantial margin – even when employing relatively simple features. Our findings suggest that unsupervised data acquisition strategies should be explicitly guided by techniques that aim to match these meta-properties, ultimately yielding more effective WSD systems.

These platforms are not merely channels for broadcasting messages, but dynamic ecosystems where opinions are formed, shared, and, critically, *influenced*. Understanding the mechanisms driving this influence is paramount for businesses seeking to gauge consumer sentiment, predict future trends, and tailor their strategies accordingly. The study of opinion dynamics, therefore, has emerged as a vital area of research within the intersection of social computing, network science, and natural language processing. Traditional approaches to modeling opinion formation have largely treated opinions as either discrete categories (e.g., positive, negative, neutral) or continuous values representing sentiment strength. While these approaches provide valuable insights, they often fall short of capturing the nuanced semantic content underlying opinions and the complex interplay between content, social connections, and individual beliefs. For instance, two users expressing "positive" sentiment towards a product may do so for fundamentally different reasons, highlighting the importance of understanding the *why* behind the opinion, not just *that* it exists. response: Documenting the world’s linguistic diversity is a critical endeavor, yet it is frequently hampered by the resource constraints faced by field linguists. These linguists, working directly with native speakers, are responsible for eliciting, recording, and analyzing language data – a process vital for both theoretical linguistic understanding and language preservation. A core component of this documentation is syntactic annotation, which involves identifying the grammatical relationships between words in a sentence, typically represented as a dependency parse. However, manual syntactic annotation is a time-consuming and labor-intensive process, requiring substantial linguistic expertise. The slow pace of annotation limits the amount of data that can be analyzed, hindering progress in understanding the target language’s structure and ultimately impacting documentation efforts. Therefore, automating or semi-automating syntactic annotation is a key challenge in field linguistics. Recent advances in Natural Language Processing (NLP) offer promising tools to address this challenge. Dependency parsing, in particular, has matured significantly, with highly accurate parsers available for resource-rich languages like English and Chinese. However, these pre-trained parsers are largely ineffective for low-resource languages – the vast majority of the world’s languages – as they lack the necessary training data. This necessitates the development of methods for rapidly adapting and learning parsers with minimal supervision, directly within the field linguistic context. This paper presents experiments focusing on incrementally learning a dependency parser to support language documentation in field linguistics. Our work is motivated by the need to develop tools that can assist linguists in annotating syntactic structure quickly and accurately, even with extremely limited training data. We aim to dramatically reduce annotation time by leveraging the power of machine learning, thereby accelerating the entire language documentation process. We present a new parallel corpus specifically designed to facilitate the development of such a parser. This corpus comprises descriptions of spatial relations and motion events, elicited through the use of pictures and video clips – a standard technique used by field linguists to prompt language production from native speakers. Descriptions were collected in four languages: English, Spanish, German, and Egyptian Arabic, providing a diverse dataset for training and evaluation. The parallel nature of the corpus allows for cross-lingual transfer learning and more robust model development. We compare the performance of two popular dependency parsing frameworks, MSTParser (McDonald et al., 2006) and MaltParser (Nivre et al., 2006), when trained on small subsets of this corpus. Our results demonstrate that MaltParser consistently achieves superior performance, particularly in low-data regimes. Critically, we also present experiments evaluating the use of the learned parser as an annotation aid. We find that even a parser trained on as little as a single sentence from the corpus can significantly reduce annotation time, highlighting the potential for rapid adaptation and practical impact in field linguistic settings. This suggests that even minimal initial annotation effort can yield substantial benefits in accelerating the documentation process. This research contributes to a growing body of work focused on adapting NLP techniques for low-resource language documentation, with a particular emphasis on creating a practical tool for field linguists.

Despite the inherent ambiguity of natural language, and the potential for misinterpretation, people routinely convey complex ideas to one another with surprising ease. A cornerstone of our understanding of this efficiency is the work of Paul Grice (1975), who proposed that successful communication relies on a “cooperative principle”: speakers and listeners assume each other are, and will be, cooperative in the exchange of information. This principle manifests as a set of conversational maxims—quality (be truthful), quantity (be informative but not overly so), relevance (be relevant), and manner (be clear)—that guide the production and interpretation of utterances. While Grice’s framework provides a compelling description of communicative behavior, it remains largely a *descriptive* account, lacking a foundational explanation of *why* these seemingly arbitrary principles emerge in the first place. While supervised approaches to coreference resolution have achieved high accuracy, they require large amounts of manually annotated data, which is expensive and time-consuming to obtain. Consequently, unsupervised coreference resolution remains a challenging but important research area. Existing unsupervised methods typically rely on pairwise comparisons between mentions, utilizing features such as string similarity, syntactic features, and semantic similarity (Soon et al., 2001;da Cunha et al., 2009;Bengtson and Kanazawa, 2010). response: The field of Natural Language Processing (NLP) has seen a dramatic shift in recent years, largely driven by the success of deep learning models. However, a persistent challenge remains: effectively representing linguistic information in a way that is both informative and computationally tractable. While one-hot encodings have long been a mainstay, representing each linguistic unit as a unique, independent symbol, they suffer from limitations stemming from a lack of inherent structural knowledge (Bengio et al., 2003). More recently, character-based models have emerged as a powerful alternative, leveraging the sequential nature of text and implicitly capturing some sub-lexical information (Sutskever et al., 2014; Cho et al., 2014). However, these character-based models often require significant amounts of data to learn meaningful representations, and the learned representations can be difficult to interpret. We argue that explicitly incorporating linguistically motivated features can provide a principled and efficient pathway to richer representations, particularly for languages with limited resources. This approach leverages prior linguistic knowledge to guide the learning process, resulting in more robust and interpretable models. In phonology, for example, rather than treating each phoneme (represented by an IPA symbol) as an independent unit, we can represent it in terms of its articulatory properties – how it is produced by the vocal tract. These articulatory features capture inherent relationships between sounds, allowing a model to generalize more effectively and to transfer knowledge between related languages. This paper introduces PanPhon, a novel resource designed specifically to facilitate the integration of articulatory features into NLP models. PanPhon is a database linking over 5,000 International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) segments to 21 carefully selected subsegmental articulatory features. These features are based on established phonetic theory and describe aspects such as place of articulation, manner of articulation, and voicing. The goal of PanPhon is to provide a bridge between the abstract representations used in computational linguistics and the concrete, physical realities of speech production. We demonstrate the utility of PanPhon through a series of experiments focusing on Named Entity Recognition (NER) and Orthography-to-IPA conversion. We show that neural Conditional Random Field (CRF) models incorporating PanPhon features achieve performance comparable to character-based models on monolingual NER tasks in Spanish and Turkish. More significantly, on cross-lingual transfer tasks (specifically, from Uzbek to Turkish), PanPhon-enhanced models demonstrably outperform their character-based counterparts. This result highlights the key advantage of linguistically-informed representations: their ability to generalize more effectively across languages with shared phonetic properties. Moreover, the inclusion of PanPhon features provides measurable improvements in Orthography-to-IPA conversion, further demonstrating its versatility. This work is intended to serve as a valuable resource for the NLP community, fostering the development of more robust, interpretable, and data-efficient language processing systems. Determining *what* people are talking about is often as important as determining *how* they feel about it. For example, in a restaurant review, identifying aspects like “food quality,” “service,” and “ambiance” allows for a more nuanced understanding of customer opinions than simply knowing the overall sentiment is positive or negative. A common approach to aspect extraction leverages unsupervised topic modeling techniques, such as Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) (Blei et al., 2003). These methods effectively discover latent topics within a corpus of text, which can often correspond to meaningful aspects of the entities being discussed. However, a significant challenge with applying topic models directly to aspect extraction lies in their tendency to produce incoherent or semantically overlapping topics, particularly when dealing with large and diverse datasets. The discovered topics frequently lack clear interpretability and may not align well with human-defined aspects, hindering downstream sentiment analysis tasks. To address this issue of topic incoherence, researchers have turned to knowledge-based approaches, incorporating prior knowledge about potential aspects to guide the topic modeling process. These approaches typically rely on manually curated lexicons or ontologies, providing the topic model with seed words or constraints that encourage the discovery of more focused and interpretable topics (Titov & McDonald, 2008; Mei et al., 2007). A widely adopted paradigm involves scoring candidate parse trees using a linear model that combines weighted features representing various aspects of the parse. The efficacy of these models hinges on the design of informative features, which are traditionally crafted by linguistic experts. These features are typically defined using templates – parameterized rules applied to portions of the dependency tree, extracting properties such as the word form, part-of-speech tag, or dependency relation. However, the space of possible feature combinations defined by these templates is vast. response: Knowledge Base Population (KBP) is a critical task in natural language processing, aiming to automatically populate knowledge bases (KBs) with facts extracted from unstructured text. Populating KBs is crucial for a wide range of applications, including question answering, information retrieval, and reasoning. The task typically involves identifying entities, relations, and their corresponding values within text, and then linking these extracted pieces of information to existing entities in a KB. Two prominent tasks within KBP are Cold Start Slot Filling (CSSF) and Tri-lingual Entity Discovery and Linking (TEDL). CSSF addresses the challenge of predicting values for slots of entities that have limited prior information in the KB – the “cold start” problem. TEDL, on the other hand, focuses on discovering new entities mentioned in text across multiple languages and linking them to existing entities in a multilingual KB. Both CSSF and TEDL represent significant challenges for NLP systems. CSSF necessitates robust generalization capabilities to infer slot values for entities with sparse KB entries, often relying on contextual clues and distant supervision. TEDL, further complicated by multilingual data, requires effective cross-lingual entity alignment and disambiguation. In recent years, a diverse range of approaches have been explored for these tasks, spanning rule-based methods, supervised machine learning models, and distant supervision techniques (Riedel et al., 2013; Mintz et al., 2009; Hoffart et al., 2011). A common strategy for improving performance on KBP tasks is to combine multiple systems, effectively leveraging the complementary strengths of different approaches. Ensembling, a technique that aggregates predictions from multiple models, has consistently demonstrated its effectiveness in various NLP tasks (Dietterich, 2000). Traditional ensembling methods include averaging predictions, weighted averaging, and stacking (Wolpert, 1992). However, designing effective ensembling strategies can be non-trivial, particularly when integrating systems with varying levels of performance and differing underlying assumptions. Our approach moves beyond simple averaging or stacking, and intelligently leverages the outputs of both explicitly trained systems and systems derived from unsupervised learning techniques. We demonstrate that our combined approach significantly outperforms the best system from the 2015 KBP competition, several standard ensembling baselines, and a sophisticated state-of-the-art stacking method. The consistent success across two distinct and demanding KBP tasks highlights the power and generality of our technique. This work contributes a new and effective ensembling method for KBP, showcasing the potential of strategically integrating supervised and unsupervised learning for enhanced knowledge base construction. response: Distributed representations of words, also known as word embeddings, have become a cornerstone of modern natural language processing (NLP). Introduced initially by (Bengio et al., 2003; Mikolov et al., 2013; Pennington et al., 2014), these representations map words from a high-dimensional, sparse space (e.g., one-hot encoding) to a lower-dimensional, dense vector space. This mapping captures semantic and syntactic relationships between words, enabling effective generalization and improved performance on a plethora of NLP tasks, including part-of-speech tagging, named entity recognition, and sentiment analysis. A key advantage of distributed representations is their ability to mitigate data sparsity issues inherent in supervised learning. Traditional methods relying on discrete features often struggle when encountering unseen or rare words. Word embeddings, trained on large amounts of unlabeled text, provide a means to represent even infrequent words within a meaningful semantic space. The effectiveness of these representations hinges on the availability of substantial unlabeled text data for training. Fortunately, such data is readily accessible for many languages, fueling the rapid adoption of word embeddings across diverse NLP applications. However, the majority of research has focused on inducing representations for individual languages in isolation. This presents a challenge for crosslingual NLP, where the goal is to leverage knowledge learned in one language to improve performance in another—particularly important for low-resource languages where labeled data is scarce. Traditional approaches to crosslingual NLP often rely on machine translation (MT) to bridge the linguistic gap. While effective, MT systems are complex, computationally intensive, and can introduce errors that propagate through the pipeline. This capability holds promise for a diverse range of applications, including personalized communication, text simplification, and creative writing assistance. For instance, one might wish to transform a casual online comment into a more professional email, or to adapt a complex scientific article for a broader, less technically-inclined audience. While the potential benefits are significant, progress in style transfer has been hampered by a critical bottleneck: the scarcity of well-constructed datasets, robust evaluation benchmarks, and reliable automatic metrics. Existing datasets for style transfer often focus on narrow domains or employ relatively small corpora, limiting the generalizability of learned models. Furthermore, the subjective nature of style makes evaluation particularly challenging. Automatic metrics, while offering a scalable alternative, frequently fail to correlate well with human judgments, leading to misleading conclusions about the effectiveness of style transfer systems. response: The meaning of words is far from static. While traditional lexical resources like WordNet offer a foundational understanding of word senses, they often fall short when applied to the dynamic and nuanced language used within specific communities or domains (Kulkarni et al., 2013). The same term can carry drastically different connotations and semantic weight depending on the context of its usage. For instance, the word “sick” in general English denotes illness, but within certain online communities, it's a positive expression denoting something impressive or cool. Similarly, “shade” in mainstream usage refers to partial darkness, but in online discourse, it signifies subtle, indirect disrespect. Recognizing and capturing these domain-specific semantic variations is therefore crucial for numerous NLP tasks, including sentiment analysis, topic modeling, and information retrieval. Existing approaches to address this challenge often rely on sentiment analysis techniques or the creation of domain-specific lexicons (Liu, 2012;Turney, 2002). While effective for polarity detection, these methods frequently overlook the broader spectrum of semantic dimensions beyond simply positive or negative. More sophisticated techniques leverage distributional semantics, representing words as vectors in high-dimensional space where semantic similarity is reflected in proximity (Mikolov et al., 2013;Pennington et al., 2014). However, these vector spaces often encode a general-purpose semantics, requiring adaptation or fine-tuning for specific domains. response: Paraphrase generation, the task of expressing the same meaning using different words, is a core problem in natural language processing with applications ranging from text simplification and machine translation to dialogue systems and information retrieval. Traditionally, paraphrase generation has relied on rule-based systems utilizing lexical resources like WordNet (Lavie, 2008; Ganitlar & Lam, 2009). However, these approaches often struggle with scalability and require extensive manual effort. More recently, statistical machine translation (SMT) techniques have been applied to paraphrase generation, treating the source sentence as a “foreign” language and the target paraphrase as its translation (Zhao et al., 2008; Wubben et al., 2012). While showing improvement over rule-based systems, SMT approaches are limited by their reliance on parallel corpora of paraphrases, which are scarce. The advent of deep learning, particularly sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models with attention mechanisms (Bahdanau et al., 2014; Sutskever et al., 2014), has revolutionized machine translation and, subsequently, paraphrase generation. These models learn to map input sequences to output sequences, making them well-suited for generating paraphrases. However, a crucial limitation of these models is their tendency to *memorize* patterns from the training data rather than genuinely *understanding* the underlying semantics (Lipton et al., 2016). This memorization manifests as a propensity to generate grammatically correct but semantically inappropriate paraphrases—essentially, repeating phrases or structures from the training set without capturing the original sentence's meaning. To mitigate this issue, we propose a novel encoder-decoder framework named the Word Embedding Attention Network (WEAN). Unlike conventional seq2seq models that predict words directly from a fixed vocabulary, WEAN generates words by *querying* distributed word representations. Specifically, the decoder uses the encoded sentence representation to query a space of pre-trained word embeddings (e.g., GloVe, Word2Vec) for words that are semantically appropriate in the context of the current decoding step. The core idea is that by operating in a continuous embedding space, the model can better capture semantic relationships and generate more meaningful paraphrases. This approach moves beyond simple word-level predictions and encourages the model to truly reason about the meaning of the words it generates. Several approaches have been proposed to tackle this challenge, including feature adaptation (Blitzer et al., 2006;Glorot et al., 2011), instance weighting (Dai et al., 2014), and domain-invariant representation learning (Glorot et al., 2011;Chen et al., 2013). response: The demand for automated writing assistance tools has grown significantly with the increasing number of non-native English speakers participating in global communication. A key component of such tools is the ability to automatically detect and correct grammatical errors in learner writing. While substantial progress has been made in the development of such systems, challenges remain, specifically in achieving robustness and accuracy when dealing with the varied and often unpredictable errors produced by language learners (Polio, 2010). Traditional approaches to grammatical error correction (GEC) often rely on large, natively written corpora to build language models (LM) or train error-specific classifiers. Language models, for example, can identify grammatically implausible sequences by assigning low probabilities to incorrect phrases. Similarly, classifiers can be trained to recognize specific error types, such as incorrect article usage or preposition choices (Lee & Seneff, 2004). However, these approaches can struggle to generalize to the unique error patterns exhibited by learners, which often differ substantially from the types of errors found in native writing. Learners frequently make errors rooted in their L1 interference, overgeneralization of rules, or a lack of understanding of nuanced grammatical concepts, mistakes rarely seen in native speech or writing. Recent work has explored the use of error-annotated learner corpora for GEC (Foster et al., 2011; Han et al., 2013). However, the creation of such corpora is a time-consuming and expensive process, limiting the amount of training data available. This paper investigates a novel meta-classification approach that aims to bridge the gap between leveraging the abundance of natively written data and effectively adapting to the characteristics of learner writing. Our core idea is to combine the strengths of both language models and error-specific classifiers, trained primarily on native data, with a meta-classifier trained on a smaller corpus of error-annotated learner data. The language model and classifiers serve as feature extractors, providing evidence regarding the likelihood of various corrections, while the meta-classifier learns to optimally weight and combine this evidence to make accurate error detection and correction decisions specifically for learner writing. We focus specifically on two common error types—article and preposition errors—and evaluate our approach on a large, publicly available corpus of learner English. We compare the performance of our meta-classification approach to two baselines: a traditional language model approach and a system relying solely on error-specific classifiers. Our results demonstrate that the meta-classification approach consistently outperforms both baselines, achieving substantial gains in both error detection and correction accuracy. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of the size of the error-annotated learner corpus used to train the meta-classifier, determining the minimum amount of data required to observe significant improvements in performance. This investigation provides valuable insights into the trade-off between annotation cost and system accuracy, guiding future efforts in the development of effective GEC systems for non-native speakers. However, learning accurate PCFGs from treebanks is notoriously difficult, particularly for languages with complex, long-distance dependencies. The automatically induced latent variable grammars of Petrov et al. (2006) offer a compelling alternative, framing the PCFG learning problem as an instance of unsupervised parameter estimation. response: N-gram language models (LMs) are a cornerstone of modern natural language processing, serving as crucial components in a wide range of applications, including speech recognition (Jelinek, 1976), machine translation (Brown et al., 1993), and text generation (Rosenblatt, 2011). At their core, these models estimate the probability of a sequence of words, allowing systems to predict the likelihood of various continuations given a context. However, the efficacy of N-gram LMs is inextricably linked to the size of the corpus used for training. As the training corpus grows – a trend driven by the increasing availability of text data – the size of the language model itself swells dramatically. This growth in model size poses significant challenges, particularly in resource-constrained environments such as mobile devices or embedded systems. Large models demand substantial memory for storage, and their computational complexity can hinder real-time performance. Traditional implementations of N-gram LMs often rely on tree-based structures, like tries or suffix trees, to efficiently store and retrieve N-gram probabilities. However, these structures can become excessively large as the vocabulary size and N-gram order increase. Recent research has explored alternative data structures and compression techniques to mitigate these issues. For example, quantitative variable precision (QVP) (Goodman, 2001) and Bloom filters (Bloom, 1970) have been employed to reduce model size, although they may introduce approximation errors. Weighted finite-state transducers (WFSTs) (Mohri, 1997) offer a powerful framework for representing and composing LMs, but can be complex to implement and manage. response: Understanding how the meanings of words evolve over time – a phenomenon known as semantic shift – is a core problem in historical linguistics, cognitive science, and increasingly, computational linguistics. The study of semantic shift provides insights into cultural change, the dynamics of language use, and the cognitive processes underlying meaning construction. Traditionally, historical linguists have relied on meticulous manual analysis of texts across different time periods to trace these changes (Haspelmath, 2004). However, the advent of large historical corpora has opened up new avenues for investigating semantic shift using quantitative methods. Diachronic distributional semantics (Michel et al., 2005; Hamilton et al., 2016) has emerged as a prominent approach in this domain. These models leverage the distributional hypothesis – the idea that words that occur in similar contexts tend to have similar meanings – but extend it to consider context *across time*. By analyzing changes in a word’s distributional profile over time, researchers can identify shifts in its semantic usage. Early work often involved comparing distributional representations at discrete time slices, analyzing changes in nearest neighbors, or modeling word embeddings as time series (Hamilton et al., 2016). However, existing approaches face several limitations. Treating time as discrete can lead to a loss of information about the gradual nature of semantic change. Modeling semantic shifts as time series requires careful selection of time intervals and can struggle to capture non-linear changes. Moreover, evaluating the performance of diachronic models and quantitatively assessing their ability to capture the intricacies of semantic trajectories has proven challenging. In this paper, we propose a novel deep neural network framework for modeling semantic shift. Our approach departs from traditional time series modeling by representing time as a *continuous* variable and modeling a word’s usage as a function of time. Specifically, we employ a neural network that maps a word’s context to a latent semantic space, while simultaneously incorporating temporal information to predict the semantic representation at any given point in time. This allows us to capture nuanced and potentially non-linear patterns of semantic change. To facilitate rigorous evaluation, we introduce a new synthetic task designed to specifically measure a model’s ability to reconstruct the semantic trajectory of a word. This task allows us to quantitatively assess how well our model captures the dynamic evolution of word meaning. Beyond simply detecting change, our model provides a continuous representation of semantic space across time, opening possibilities for analyzing the *speed* of lexical change. We investigate whether the derivatives of our model’s output can be meaningfully correlated with the rate at which a word’s meaning is shifting. Through experiments, we demonstrate that our deep neural model consistently outperforms existing diachronic distributional models on our novel synthetic task, and shows promising results in capturing known patterns of semantic shift in historical text. Phrase-based SMT (Koehn et al., 2003; Marcu et al., 2006) specifically, has proven remarkably effective, leveraging phrases as the fundamental unit of translation, and achieving state-of-the-art results for many language pairs. However, a fundamental limitation of phrase-based systems lies in the independence assumption amongst phrases. Each phrase is modeled independently of its surrounding context, hindering the system's ability to capture long-range dependencies and leading to disfluent or inaccurate translations, especially when dealing with complex sentence structures or ambiguous words. Recent advances in neural network modeling have demonstrated significant potential for addressing the shortcomings of SMT (Cho et al., 2014; Sutskever et al., 2014; Bahdanau et al., 2015). Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), in particular, excel at processing sequential data and capturing contextual information. Sequence-to-sequence models with attention mechanisms have achieved compelling results, often surpassing phrase-based systems in terms of translation fluency. However, these end-to-end neural machine translation (NMT) systems still grapple with challenges related to rare words and the ability to effectively leverage existing phrase tables painstakingly constructed over years of research. First, we propose a factorization of the bilingual tuples into independent source and target representations, drastically reducing the number of parameters and improving generalization. Second, we decompose phrasal tuples into word-level representations, further refining the model and providing richer contextual information. These models represent words as dense vectors in a high-dimensional space, where semantic similarity is mirrored by closeness in vector space—i.e., words used in similar contexts tend to have similar vector representations (Pennington et al., 2014; Mikolov et al., 2013). However, a fundamental limitation of standard VSMs is their inability to effectively differentiate between synonymous and antonymous relationships. In a purely distributional setting, words appearing in opposing contexts (e.g., “good” and “bad”) can exhibit high vector space similarity due to the shared presence of certain words (e.g., modifiers such as "very", "not"). This limitation hinders tasks requiring nuanced semantic understanding, such as sentiment analysis and text classification. Existing approaches to address this problem often involve incorporating external lexical resources, such as WordNet (Miller, 1995), into VSMs. These methods typically augment the vector representation of a word with information about its synsets and hypernyms, or use lexical relations to refine similarity measures. While significant progress has been made in areas like speech recognition and natural language understanding, a critical gap remains in bridging the semantic gap between human intention, expressed as high-level instructions, and the concrete actions required to fulfill that intention within a dynamic environment. Consider the simple instruction: “Bring me the book on the table.” A human effortlessly understands this instruction, recognizing the implicit sub-goals – locating the table, identifying the book, navigating to the book, grasping the book, and transporting it to the speaker – and the appropriate sequence of actions to achieve them. However, for a robotic agent or software assistant, directly translating this instruction into a sequence of executable commands is a substantial challenge. Existing approaches to instruction following often rely on pre-defined templates or hand-crafted rules that map specific keywords to predefined actions. These methods, while effective in limited domains, struggle with the inherent flexibility and ambiguity of natural language. Furthermore, they necessitate extensive manual effort to adapt to new environments or tasks. Statistical machine translation techniques, treating instructions as source language and commands as target language, have shown promise, but they typically require large parallel corpora of instruction-command pairs – a resource that is often unavailable or expensive to create. Crucially, these methods lack the ability to *reason* about the environment and infer the missing steps necessary to achieve a given goal. They leave unstated the necessary preconditions, intermediate steps, and the effects of actions within the environment. To bridge this gap, a system must possess an internal model of the environment that allows it to predict the consequences of its actions and plan a sequence of commands that will lead to the desired outcome. Unlike traditional syntactic parse trees, AMR focuses on “who is doing what to whom,” representing concepts as nodes and semantic relations as directed edges. This rich semantic structure makes AMR a valuable resource for a variety of natural language processing tasks, including machine translation, information extraction, and question answering. However, automatically constructing AMR graphs from raw text is a challenging problem. Early approaches to AMR parsing relied heavily on feature engineering and complex graph alignment techniques (Gildea and Jurafsky, 2000; Kyle and Van Genuchten, 2008). response: Understanding the structure of text is a fundamental challenge in natural language processing. While content-based approaches have dominated much of the field, focusing on the semantic meaning of words and phrases, a growing body of work recognizes the importance of *structural* cues in determining how humans understand and process text (Mann and Thompson, 1988;Halliday and Hasan, 1976). These cues, often manifested in rhetorical relationships between sentences and paragraphs, provide a scaffolding for interpretation, enabling readers to navigate and comprehend even lengthy and complex documents. Traditional methods for analyzing text structure, such as Rhetorical Structure Theory (RST) (Mann and Thompson, 1988), require extensive manual annotation, are computationally expensive, and don’t scale effectively to large corpora. Consequently, automated techniques for identifying and leveraging structural information remain a significant area of research. Existing approaches to identifying important textual units often rely on content-driven metrics like Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF) (Robertson, 2004). While TF-IDF effectively captures the statistical importance of words in a corpus, it fundamentally overlooks the role of structural features. A word might frequently appear in a document, but that doesn’t necessarily mean it’s structurally important—it might simply be a common function word or a frequently used topic-specific term. Similarly, while topic modeling (Blei et al., 2003) can uncover latent thematic structure, it rarely explicitly models the rhetorical relationships that organize a text. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to measuring structural importance, termed the Rhetorical Structure Index (RSI). RSI aims to identify words and phrases that act as structural cues within a document, independent of their specific semantic content. Our core idea is that words or phrases that consistently appear at the beginning or end of segments, or in positions that signal transitions in thought, are likely to be structurally important. Unlike TF-IDF, RSI doesn’t depend on term frequency or document prevalence, but instead focuses on positional patterns within the text. We hypothesize that these structurally motivated features are more informative for tasks requiring understanding of document organization – such as segmenting unstructured lecture transcripts into coherent sections. Our results highlight the value of attending to the “how” of writing—the rhetorical structure—in addition to the “what” of writing—the content itself. These initial findings pave the way for further exploration into the broader applications of RSI and the development of more sophisticated techniques for extracting and utilizing structural information from text.

This burgeoning field draws from natural language processing, artificial intelligence, and logic, offering potential applications in areas ranging from legal reasoning and policy analysis to online debate moderation and persuasive technology. Historically, approaches to AM have relied heavily on hand-engineered features derived from linguistic theory and argumentation schemes (e.g., Toulmin’s model of argument – Toulmin, 1958). These features often target the identification of argument components – claims, premises, and their relationships – and require significant domain expertise to design and implement effectively. Initial efforts focused on representing arguments as distributed vectors and employing these embeddings for classification tasks (e.g., Niculae and Banea, 2017). However, these approaches often operate at the argument component level, requiring a pre-defined segmentation of the text into claims and premises, a task in itself prone to error. Furthermore, they may struggle to capture the intricate relationships between argumentative elements and the long-range dependencies inherent in complex arguments. In this paper, we explore the potential of neural end-to-end learning for AM, moving away from feature engineering and component-level analysis. We investigate two distinct neural formulations: framing AM as a token-based dependency parsing problem and as a token-based sequence tagging problem. response: The WordNet lexicon (Fellbaum, 1998) has long served as a cornerstone resource for natural language processing, providing a structured representation of lexical semantics through synonym sets (synsets) linked by semantic relations such as hypernymy (is-a) and meronymy (part-of). However, even this extensive resource is inherently incomplete. The lexicon lacks coverage for emerging concepts, particularly those arising in specialized domains, and often suffers from a lack of fine-grained attributes that would allow for more nuanced semantic understanding. Manually extending WordNet remains a labor-intensive and expensive process, necessitating the development of automated approaches. Previous efforts to augment WordNet have explored a range of techniques, often relying on distributional semantics and co-occurrence statistics (Lin et al., 1998; Pantel and Hovy, 2003; Gabrilovich and Markovitch, 2007). These approaches typically identify potential attributes – or “properties” – based on patterns observed in large text corpora. For instance, one method might identify “has_color: red” as an attribute of “apple” by observing frequent co-occurrence of those terms. While successful to a degree, these heuristic methods often struggle with precision, generating numerous irrelevant or noisy attribute suggestions. A fundamental limitation is the reliance on surface-level co-occurrence, without a robust probabilistic framework to model the underlying relationship between concepts and attributes. In this paper, we address the problem of concept-attribute attachment by introducing a suite of Bayesian models based on Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) (Blei et al., 2003). LDA has proven remarkably effective in topic modeling, uncovering latent semantic structure in text collections. We leverage this capability to model the relationship between WordNet concepts and a broad range of potential attributes, framing the problem as one of discovering latent topics that connect concepts to their properties. Our models allow us to both rank candidate attributes for a given concept – providing a prioritized list for potential manual review – and directly assign attributes to concepts with associated probabilities. response: Statistical machine translation (SMT) has achieved remarkable success in recent years, largely driven by the phrase-based approach (Koehn et al., 2003). These systems learn to translate phrases – sequences of words – from a source language to a target language, composing the final translation from these learned phrase pairs. However, a key limitation of standard phrase-based SMT, particularly when translating *into* morphologically rich languages, is the issue of data sparsity (Knight et al., 1999;Nelken & Yarowsky, 2005). Morphologically rich languages, such as Arabic, Turkish, and Finnish, generate a large number of distinct word forms from a relatively small number of morphemes. This leads to a combinatorial explosion of possible word forms in the target language, which standard SMT models struggle to adequately represent due to insufficient parallel training data. A common approach to alleviate this sparsity is morphological segmentation (Creutz & Lagus, 2005;Popović & Ney, 2015), where words are broken down into their constituent morphemes. This dramatically reduces the vocabulary size and allows the model to generalize more effectively to unseen word forms. However, introducing segmentation also necessitates a *desegmentation* step – reassembling the morphemes into surface-level words – to produce fluent, readable output. Traditionally, this desegmentation is performed as a post-processing step, typically using a 1-best segmentation approach (e.g., using Maximum a Posteriori (MAP) estimation). While conceptually simple, this post-hoc desegmentation introduces several drawbacks. Firstly, it restricts the search space during decoding, preventing the decoder from exploring alternative segmentations that might lead to a better overall translation. Secondly, the decoder is unable to directly optimize for the quality of the final, desegmented output, as the scoring function only considers the segmented forms. For example, a word-level language model (WM) – a crucial component in modern SMT systems – cannot be applied to the final, fluent target sentence if the decoder only has access to segmented morphemes. In this paper, we present a novel approach to address these limitations: *decoder-integrated desegmentation*. Our method incorporates the desegmentation process directly into the phrase-based decoding search, allowing the decoder to explore different segmentation options and score them based on features that consider the final, desegmented target. This enables the use of powerful features, such as a surface-level word language model, throughout the entire search process, leading to improved translation quality. We achieve this by extending the standard phrase-based decoder to handle multiple segmentation hypotheses simultaneously, scoring them based on both translation model scores and a desegmentation model that favors fluent, grammatical word forms. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a large-scale English to Arabic translation task. Our experiments show a significant improvement over a strong 1-best desegmentation baseline, highlighting the benefits of integrating desegmentation directly into the decoding process. Our results confirm the importance of considering the final, desegmented target during the search process and pave the way for more sophisticated approaches to handling morphological complexity in statistical machine translation.

response: Automated essay scoring (AES) has a long history in educational testing and assessment. For decades, AES systems have been used to provide rapid, consistent, and cost-effective feedback on student writing. Early AES systems relied heavily on hand-crafted features – measures of essay length, vocabulary richness, grammatical correctness, and rhetorical structure – combined with linear regression models. While these systems achieved reasonable levels of agreement with human raters, their performance was fundamentally limited by the quality and completeness of the hand-engineered features. The process of feature engineering is time-consuming, requiring substantial domain expertise in both natural language processing and educational assessment. Furthermore, the features that prove most predictive of essay quality can vary across different writing prompts, genres, and educational levels, necessitating a continuous cycle of feature refinement. More recently, machine learning techniques, such as Support Vector Regression (SVR) and Gradient Boosting, have been applied to AES, often leveraging larger feature sets and more sophisticated learning algorithms. However, these systems still rely on expertly designed features and struggle to generalize to unseen prompts or essay populations. The recent resurgence of deep learning has opened up new possibilities for AES. Deep neural networks, particularly recurrent neural networks (RNNs), are capable of learning complex patterns and representations directly from raw text data, without the need for explicit feature engineering. This is particularly appealing for AES, where the nuances of writing quality are often difficult to capture with traditional features. The ability of RNNs to process sequential data makes them well-suited for modeling the structure and coherence of an essay, capturing dependencies between sentences and paragraphs. In this paper, we present a novel approach to AES based on recurrent neural networks, specifically Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks. Our goal is to demonstrate that a deep learning model, trained directly on essay text and associated scores, can achieve state-of-the-art performance without relying on manually engineered features. We explore several variations of RNN architectures, and provide an analysis of the learned representations to gain insights into how the model perceives and evaluates essay quality. Our experimental results, evaluated on a standard AES dataset, demonstrate that our LSTM-based system significantly outperforms a strong baseline system relying on traditional features, achieving a noteworthy improvement in inter-rater agreement as measured by Quadratic Weighted Kappa. response: Question Answering (QA) systems are increasingly expected to not only provide correct answers but also to understand the temporal context surrounding those answers. Many real-world questions necessitate reasoning about *when* events occurred, their durations, and the relationships between them. For example, questions like “When did Apple release the first iPhone?” or “What happened before the French Revolution?” require explicit temporal reasoning capabilities beyond simple keyword matching. Consequently, Temporal Information Extraction (TIE) – the task of identifying and classifying temporal expressions and relations within text – has become a crucial component of advanced QA systems (Ferretti et al., 2009;Ning et al., 2018). Early approaches to TIE relied heavily on hand-crafted rules and feature engineering (Allan, 2008;Verhagen et al., 2009). These systems, while achieving reasonable performance, suffered from limited generalizability and required significant human effort to adapt to new domains. More recently, machine learning techniques, particularly those leveraging distributed word representations and recurrent neural networks (RNNs), have demonstrated significant improvements in TIE performance (Lample et al., 2016;Zhou et al., 2016;Manabu et al., 2018). However, many existing neural models struggle to effectively capture long-range dependencies and nuanced temporal relationships, especially those spanning multiple sentences or even entire documents. A key observation is that temporal relations are rarely expressed in isolation. Instead, they are often signaled by syntactic structures connecting the involved entities and temporal expressions. For instance, prepositional phrases like “after,” “before,” or “during” directly indicate temporal relationships. Similarly, verb tense and aspect frequently provide crucial clues about the timing of events. Exploiting syntactic dependencies, therefore, appears essential for robust TIE. Existing work often incorporates syntactic information as additional features into neural networks (Kazemzadeh et al., 2013;Li et al., 2017), but typically does so in a limited and feature-engineered manner. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to TIE that leverages syntactic dependencies more directly within a uniform, LSTM-based architectural framework. Our core idea is to encode the shortest dependency path between event entities as input to a series of LSTMs trained to classify various types of temporal relations: intra-sentence relations (occurring within a single sentence), cross-sentence relations (spanning multiple sentences), and document creation time. This concise representation effectively captures the syntactic context crucial for accurate relation identification. Furthermore, we introduce a “double-checking” technique that reverses the order of entity pairs during classification, significantly improving recall, and a global pruning algorithm to resolve potential conflicts. Our approach yields state-of-the-art results on the QA-TempEval dataset (SemEval 2015 Task 5), substantially outperforming previous methods. We also demonstrate the intrinsic effectiveness of our technique through evaluations on the Timebank-Dense corpus, achieving competitive performance. Through analysis and experimentation, we show that the integration of syntactic dependency paths within a simple, consistent LSTM architecture provides a powerful and effective solution for temporal information extraction, contributing significantly to the development of more sophisticated and temporally-aware QA systems.

response: Transliteration, the mapping of words from one writing system to another, is a crucial component in a diverse set of Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks. It serves as a vital bridge in machine translation (MT) for handling proper nouns and loanwords, enhances cross-lingual information retrieval (CLIR) by enabling searches across different scripts, and facilitates multilingual named entity recognition (NER). While manual transliteration lexicons offer high precision, their creation is laborious and expensive, particularly for low-resource languages or rapidly evolving terminology. Consequently, automatic transliteration mining has emerged as a compelling solution, leveraging the wealth of readily available comparable or parallel corpora. Early approaches to transliteration mining focused on string similarity measures and pattern recognition (Koehn & Knight, 2000; Al-Onaizan & Knight, 2002). More recent approaches have exploited statistical machine translation (SMT) techniques, treating transliteration as a translation problem (Gauss & Striegel, 2005; Chung et al., 2006). However, many of these methods struggle with variations in orthography, phonetic ambiguities, and the inherent noise present in noisy parallel or comparable corpora. Further, they often struggle to generalize beyond observed transliteration pairs. To address these challenges, we introduce an enhanced transliteration mining technique grounded in a generative graph reinforcement learning framework. Our approach moves beyond simple alignment techniques by explicitly modeling relationships between source and target character sequences in a bipartite graph. An initial set of transliteration mappings is learned via automatic alignment, forming the foundation of this graph. A novel reinforcement learning algorithm then iteratively refines this graph, dynamically inferring additional mappings and adjusts the weight of existing mappings based on their utility and consistency. By strategically reinforcing promising connections and penalizing noisy ones, our method effectively captures intricate transliteration patterns and improves the accuracy of mined mappings. This paper details the architecture of our graph reinforcement model, the link reweighting strategy employed, and a comprehensive evaluation across four diverse alphabet-based language pairs: English-Arabic, English-Russian, English-Hindi, and English-Tamil. Importantly, our results surpass the current state-of-the-art in transliteration mining, underscoring the effectiveness of our graph reinforcement approach. We demonstrate that a principled approach to examining and exploiting character-level relationships within parallel corpora, augmented with a reinforcement learning framework, can substantially improve the quality of mined transliteration lexicons, paving the way for advancements in a wide range of multilingual NLP applications. These results outperform the best reported results in the literature by 2.6, 4.8, 0.8, and 4.1 basis points for the four language pairs respectively.

However, automated causal relation extraction remains a notoriously difficult problem. response: Understanding how humans represent and organize lexical knowledge is a central goal in cognitive science and linguistics. A long-standing debate concerns the nature of these representations: are they based on explicit definitions and semantic features, or do they emerge from patterns of usage and co-occurrence? Distributional semantic models (DSMs) offer a compelling computational framework for exploring the latter hypothesis. The core idea behind DSMs is that the meaning of a word can be inferred from the company it keeps – that is, from the contexts in which it appears. These models, typically constructed from large text corpora, represent words as vectors in a high-dimensional space, where the similarity between vectors reflects the semantic relatedness of the corresponding words (Lenci et al., 2006; Turney & Pantel, 2010). Contemporary approaches, particularly those involving word embeddings such as Word2Vec (Mikolov et al., 2013) and GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014), have demonstrated remarkable success in capturing semantic relationships and have achieved state-of-the-art performance on a variety of lexical semantic tasks. However, a crucial question remains: to what extent do these text-based DSMs accurately reflect *human* semantic representations? While DSMs have shown impressive capabilities in replicating certain aspects of human performance, concerns have been raised regarding their ecological validity. Do the patterns of co-occurrence observed in text corpora truly mirror the mental processes involved in word meaning comprehension and representation? Recent research suggests that the relationship may not be straightforward (Bauman et al., 2014). Humans do not passively observe language; instead, they actively construct meaning based on internalized knowledge and experience. It is possible that the distributional information derived from external text corpora – while informative – is only a partial proxy for the richer, more nuanced representations stored in the mental lexicon. Specifically, we leverage a novel, extensive dataset of word associations – responses collected from human participants asked to freely associate words prompted by a given target word. These word associations arguably tap into core aspects of human semantic memory, reflecting the immediate and intuitive conceptual relationships that come to mind when thinking about a particular word. By constructing language models based on these associations, we aim to create representations that are more closely aligned with the mental lexicon than those derived from text corpora. Our results reveal a striking pattern: the internal language models consistently outperform their external counterparts, often by a substantial margin. These findings not only demonstrate the power of leveraging human behavioral data for building semantic models but also have significant theoretical implications for our understanding of how distributional knowledge is organized and utilized by people. This work challenges the prevailing assumption that large text corpora provide a complete and accurate reflection of the human mental lexicon, offering strong evidence that internal representations play a critical role in shaping our understanding of word meaning.

response: Tree kernels (TKs) have emerged as a powerful and effective technique for a wide variety of natural language processing (NLP) tasks, particularly those leveraging structured data like parse trees. Their ability to implicitly map tree structures into high-dimensional feature spaces allows them to capture rich syntactic and semantic relationships without the need for explicit feature engineering. However, this very power comes at a cost: the resulting feature space is often extremely large, making interpretation difficult and potentially hindering scalability. While TKs achieve excellent performance, understanding *why* they work – what specific substructures are driving the classification decision – remains largely a black box. This lack of interpretability limits our ability to gain insights into the underlying problem domain and can pose challenges for deploying TKs in resource-constrained environments. In this paper, we address the challenge of understanding the feature space induced by tree kernels. We present a novel framework for “reverse engineering” TK spaces, aiming to identify the most important tree fragments—subtrees—that contribute significantly to the performance of a kernel-based machine learning model, typically a Support Vector Machine (SVM). Our approach isn’t simply about identifying frequent substructures; rather, we focus on substructures deemed important *by the learned model itself*, specifically by analyzing the weights assigned to features during SVM training. The core of our method is a mining algorithm designed to extract these impactful tree fragments. This algorithm leverages the estimated weights from the trained SVM to rank substructures according to their relevance. By focusing on the features that truly influence the classification decision, we can effectively distill the essence of the TK representation. The benefits of this reverse engineering process are two-fold. First, it enhances our understanding of the target problem domain by revealing which tree patterns are most indicative of specific classes or relations. This knowledge can be invaluable for linguistic analysis and the development of more informed feature engineering strategies. Second, and crucially, it enables us to create an explicit representation of the input data based on the mined features. This explicit representation has significant practical implications. By restricting the feature space to only the most relevant substructures, we can dramatically reduce the computational cost associated with training and testing, making large-scale learning more feasible. Importantly, our experiments demonstrate that this reduction in dimensionality does *not* come at the expense of accuracy. In fact, classifiers built using the mined explicit features achieve performance comparable to traditional TK classifiers, while offering substantial improvements in training and test time. We evaluate our approach on two challenging NLP tasks – semantic role labeling and question classification – showcasing its effectiveness and versatility. Our results demonstrate that reverse engineering TK feature spaces is not only possible, but also beneficial for both interpretability and scalability. The explicit features uncovered by our method provide a window into the “mind” of the kernel machine, offering valuable insights and paving the way for more efficient and effective application of tree kernels in real-world scenarios. . . . . . . . . . .

response: Sentiment analysis, the computational task of determining the emotional tone expressed in text, has evolved considerably from document-level polarity detection to more fine-grained approaches. While traditional sentiment analysis focused on classifying an entire document as positive, negative, or neutral, it often fails to capture the nuanced opinions expressed towards specific aspects or features within that document. This limitation has fueled growing interest in aspect-level sentiment classification (ALSC), a task that aims to identify the sentiment expressed towards particular aspects of an entity mentioned in a text. For instance, in a restaurant review, a user might express positive sentiment towards the "food" but negative sentiment towards the "service." This granular level of analysis provides a more complete and insightful understanding of customer opinions and is valuable for businesses seeking to improve their products or services. Recent years have witnessed a surge in research dedicated to ALSC, with a variety of techniques being employed, ranging from lexicon-based approaches to machine learning models (Pontikis et al., 2015; Li et al., 2018). However, a key challenge in ALSC lies in effectively capturing the relationship between the target aspect and the relevant content within a sentence. The sentiment expressed towards an aspect is not simply determined by the overall sentiment of the sentence but often hinges on specific phrases or words related to that aspect. For example, consider the sentence "The appetizers are ok, but the service is slow." While the sentence contains both positive ("ok") and negative ("slow") elements, the sentiment towards “taste” (related to appetizers) is positive, while the sentiment towards “service” is negative. Existing methods often struggle to pinpoint these aspect-specific sentiment cues. Motivated by this observation, we propose an Attention-based Long Short-Term Memory Network (LSTM) for aspect-level sentiment classification. Our core hypothesis is that the significance of different words in a sentence varies depending on the specific aspect being considered. An attention mechanism allows the model to dynamically focus on the most relevant parts of the sentence when processing a particular aspect, effectively capturing the interaction between aspect and content. Unlike models that treat all words equally, our approach assigns weights to different words, highlighting those that are most indicative of the sentiment towards the target aspect. The proposed model effectively addresses the crucial task of identifying aspect-specific sentiment and leverages the strengths of both LSTMs, for sequential data modeling, and attention mechanisms, for selective focus. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through experiments on the SemEval 2014 dataset, a widely used benchmark for ALSC. The results showcase that our model not only achieves competitive performance but also establishes state-of-the-art results on this challenging task, highlighting the importance of attention mechanisms in modeling the interplay between aspects and sentiment-bearing words. This work contributes a novel neural network architecture for ALSC and provides valuable insights into the nuances of sentiment expression in relation to specific aspects within a text. response: The increasing availability of electronic health records (EHRs) presents a unique opportunity to leverage clinical text for a variety of downstream natural language processing (NLP) tasks aimed at improving healthcare. These tasks include, but are not limited to, clinical decision support, patient risk stratification, and population health management. A critical component for many of these applications is the accurate extraction and understanding of medical concepts and their relationships within clinical narratives. However, clinical text is often characterized by its unstructured nature, complex medical terminology, and the frequent use of abbreviations and synonyms. Consequently, establishing the relationships between these concepts – particularly determining when different textual mentions refer to the *same* real-world medical entity – is a challenging but crucial task. This task is known as coreference resolution. Coreference resolution, broadly defined, aims to identify all mentions in a text that refer to the same entity (Soon et al., 2001). In the medical domain, this translates to identifying mentions of the same disease, medication, symptom, or anatomical location across a patient’s medical history (Uzuner et al., 2007). For example, in the sentence “The patient was diagnosed with pneumonia and subsequently treated for the infection,” the terms “pneumonia” and “the infection” likely refer to the same medical condition. Accurate resolution of these coreferences is essential for building comprehensive patient profiles, identifying disease progression, and determining treatment effectiveness. Traditionally, coreference resolution has relied heavily on supervised learning approaches (Ng and Cardie, 2002;Denis and Baldwin, 2009). However, creating large, manually annotated corpora for medical coreference resolution is expensive, time-consuming, and requires specialized clinical expertise. This scarcity of labeled data presents a significant bottleneck for developing robust and scalable coreference systems. Semi-supervised learning methods offer a promising alternative, leveraging both labeled and unlabeled data to improve model performance. Two prominent semi-supervised techniques are co-training (Blum and Mitchell, 1998) and multi-view learning with posterior regularization (Zhu, 2005). Co-training exploits different, conditionally independent “views” of the data to iteratively train multiple classifiers, each labeling data for the others. Multi-view learning, with posterior regularization, aims to enforce consistency between predictions from multiple models trained on different views, guided by the unlabeled data. In this paper, we investigate the application of both co-training and multi-view learning with posterior regularization to the task of medical concept coreference resolution. We extract semantic and temporal features from medical concepts identified in clinical text to create these independent views. We hypothesize that the semantic context of a mention (i.e., the surrounding words and phrases) and its temporal relationship to other mentions (i.e., when it occurred in the patient's history) provide complementary information for identifying coreferent entities. We evaluate our methods on two distinct corpora of clinical text, demonstrating that these semi-supervised approaches can achieve performance approaching that of fully supervised systems, while significantly reducing the reliance on costly manual annotation.

response: Deep knowledge-based reasoning has emerged as a critical component in numerous Artificial Intelligence applications, including question answering (Bordes et al., 2013), recommendation systems (Wang et al., 2017), and automated reasoning (Rocktäschel & Serban, 2015). At the heart of these systems lies a large-scale knowledge base (KB), represented as a collection of facts or triples – typically in the form of (head entity, relation, tail entity). However, the expressive power of a KB is limited to the explicitly stated facts. To enable more sophisticated reasoning, one must infer new knowledge based on existing information. This process relies on inference formulas, logical rules that define how to derive new triples from existing ones. The creation of such formulas is traditionally a manual, knowledge engineering intensive process, proving intractable for large KBs due to the combinatorial growth of potential rules. Consequently, significant research effort has been devoted to automatically mining inference formulas from KBs. This data-driven approach bypasses the limitations of manual rule construction. Existing methods broadly fall into two categories: association rule mining (Galárraga et al., 2013) and path ranking algorithms (Lapata & Kulkarni, 2014;Paul et al., 2017). Association rule mining identifies frequent patterns in the KB, but often generates a large number of trivial or redundant rules. Path ranking algorithms, on the other hand, leverage the structural information within the KB by exploring different paths connecting entities. Random walks are particularly well-suited to traversing the graph structure of KBs, making them a popular choice for formula mining (Gardner et al., 2013;Xie et al., 2018). However, a naive application of random walks – a purely stochastic process – often suffers from low efficiency. The exploration can get “lost” in irrelevant parts of the KB, resulting in a preponderance of noisy or useless formulas. While several approaches have attempted to refine this process by introducing heuristic guidance during the random walk (Lin et al., 2018;Yang et al., 2019), these heuristics are often overly general and struggle to cope with the diverse and complex nature of potential inference rules. response: English prepositions have long presented a challenge to both language learners and computational linguists. Their polysemous nature, subtle semantic distinctions, and reliance on contextual cues for proper usage contribute to their complexity (Fillmore, 1968; Lehrer, 1990). While traditional dictionaries offer definitions, they often fall short of capturing the full range of prepositional behavior, particularly the nuanced interplay between a preposition, its object, and the surrounding syntactic context. Recent linguistic work, particularly that of Hanks (2007, 2013), has emphasized the importance of examining real-world usage patterns – “norms and exploitations” – to understand the meanings of lexical items. This approach prioritizes identifying typical contexts in which a word appears, moving beyond attempts to define meaning in isolation. Building on this theoretical framework, we introduce the Pattern Dictionary of English Prepositions (PDEP), a novel lexical resource designed to facilitate the systematic study of preposition semantics and usage. The PDEP differs significantly from existing resources in both its scope and methodology. Previous efforts, such as the PropBank corpus (Palmer et al., 2005) and FrameNet (Baker et al., 1998), while valuable, often focus on specific semantic roles or frame realizations, potentially overlooking broader patterns of prepositional behavior. Moreover, much of the available data is tagged according to pre-defined categories, which can introduce biases and limit the discovery of novel usage patterns. The PDEP, in contrast, is linked to a large corpus of 81,509 sentences encompassing 304 English prepositions, gathered under the auspices of The Preposition Project (TPP) (Hanks, 2013). Crucially, nearly 60% of these sentences (47,285) were initially *untagged*, providing a more representative sample of natural preposition use. This untagged corpus is a key innovation, enabling a data-driven approach to identifying prevalent patterns without the constraints imposed by pre-existing annotation schemes.
